generalfeedback.text:
(a) Not equal — the claim is false. \(A+B=\begin{bmatrix}a+p&b+q\\c+r&d+s\end{bmatrix}\), so \[\det(A+B)=(a+p)(d+s)-(b+q)(c+r)=ad+as+dp+ps-bc-br-cq-qr.\] But \(\det A+\det B=(ad-bc)+(ps-qr)\). These differ by the cross terms \(as+dp-br-cq\), so they are not equal in general. In words: a determinant is found by multiplying entries together, and multiplying mixes the entries of \(A\) and \(B\) — so the determinant of a sum is not the sum of the determinants. For a counterexample take \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\): then \(A+B=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\), so \(\det(A+B)=9\), but \(\det A+\det B=1+4=5\). The two sides can agree for special choices — whenever the cross terms vanish, e.g. \(B=\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\), where both sides equal \(\det A\). So a claim can fail in general yet hold in special cases.

(b) Equal — the claim is true. \({@kval@}A={@b_scal_ta@}\), so \[\det({@kval@}A)=({@kval@}a)({@kval@}d)-({@kval@}b)({@kval@}c)={@kval^2@}(ad-bc)={@kval^2@}\det A.\] Each of the two rows carries a factor \({@kval@}\), and each row contributes its own factor to the determinant, giving \({@kval@}\times{@kval@}={@kval^2@}\) — not \({@kval@}\). The same reasoning shows \(\det(kA)=k^2\det A\) for any scalar \(k\) and \(2\times2\) matrix \(A\)

(c) Not equal — the claim is false. \(A^2=\begin{bmatrix}a^2+bc&ab+bd\\ac+cd&bc+d^2\end{bmatrix}\), so \[\det(A^2)=(a^2+bc)(bc+d^2)-(ab+bd)(ac+cd)=(ad-bc)^2.\] But \(2\det A=2(ad-bc)\). Since \((ad-bc)^2\neq 2(ad-bc)\) in general, they are not equal. (In fact \(\det(A^2)=(\det A)^2\), the correct identity.) Any \(A\) whose determinant is neither \(0\) nor \(2\) is a counterexample, e.g. \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\) gives \(A^2=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\), \(\det(A^2)=1\) but \(2\det A=2\). The two sides agree exactly when \((\det A)^2=2\det A\), i.e. \(\det A(\det A-2)=0\): matrices with \(\det A=0\) or \(\det A=2\), such as \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\), are special cases where the false general claim happens to hold.

node.description: Do their matrices make the sides equal?

truefeedback.text: Indeed. \(A+B={@sum_asp@}\), so \[\det(A+B)=({@t11@})({@t22@})-({@t12@})({@t21@})={@lhs_asp@},\] while \[\det A=({@u11@})({@u22@})-({@u12@})({@u21@})={@d1_asp@},\qquad \det B=({@v11@})({@v22@})-({@v12@})({@v21@})={@d2_asp@},\] so \(\det A+\det B={@rhs_asp@}\). Both sides equal \({@lhs_asp@}\) — a special pair where the claim holds. A claim can fail in general and yet still hold for special choices; that is exactly why one counterexample disproves a "for all" statement, but one confirming example proves nothing.

Since \({@lhs_asp@}\neq{@rhs_asp@}\), this pair is not one of the special cases. Look at your expansion of \(\det(A+B)\) in the boxes above: which extra terms would need to vanish?

truefeedback.text: Indeed. \(A^2={@sq_csp@}\), so \[\det(A^2)=({@y11@})({@y22@})-({@y12@})({@y21@})={@lhs_csp@},\] while \[\det A=({@z11@})({@z22@})-({@z12@})({@z21@})={@d_csp@},\qquad\text{so}\qquad 2\det A=2\cdot{@d_csp@}={@rhs_csp@}.\] Both sides equal \({@lhs_csp@}\): your matrix has \(\det A={@d_csp@}\), and \(({@d_csp@})^2=2\cdot{@d_csp@}\). The special cases are exactly the matrices whose determinant \(x\) satisfies \(x^2=2x\) — a claim can fail in general and yet hold for special choices.
